newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi says government not at risk.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi says government not at risk.

text.p: Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi dismissed talk of early elections on Friday after the leader of the largest party in his coalition raised the prospect of instability within the government.
"The government runs absolutely no risk of elections and no one can afford them," Prodi told a reporter in response to a question. He said there was "no problem" within the coalition.
Prodi spoke amid media reports of a chill in relations between him and Massimo D'Alema's ex-communist Democratic Party of the Left (PDS) over how to deal with constitutional reform.
D'Alema warned of possible government instability -- which commentators said could lead to early elections -- in a letter published on Friday in the Rome daily La Repubblica.

"After last April's success (in national elections), we said clearly that that was not the end of the transition in Italy but that the centre-left had the duty to guarantee a decisive push towards constitutional reform," D'Alema wrote.
"Today, in the most explicit terms possible, we say that if the centre-left is not able to promote a process of reform, the stability of the government will suffer...," he added.
"Reforms are necessary and they can't be put off."
D'Alema is leading negotiations to set up a cross-party parliamentary commission to work out a much-needed reform of Italy's electoral and parliamentary system.

However, parties within Prodi's coalition are divided over what kind of reform is needed, while the opposition centre-right led by former prime minister Silvio Berlusconi wants assurances before joining any commission.
Communist Refoundation, which guarantees the government's majority in the lower house, has threatened to withdraw support if the PDS sides with the centre-right over reform.
Most newspapers on Friday ran headlines about what they said was a chilling in relations between D'Alema and Prodi over the prime minister's treatment of the opposition.
"D'Alema-Prodi, it's Cold War," Turin's La Stampa said.
PDS leaders said after a meeting of the party's executive on Thursday that Prodi should take a softer line with the opposition and seek a modus vivendi which promotes dialogue.

Some PDS leaders have accused Prodi of using terms considered too harsh, such as saying that the centre-right wanted to sabotage the government and asserting that Berlusconi was not "culturally" fit to head an eventual reform commission.
Despite his own differences with the opposition, D'Alema has been trying to keep a dialogue open with Berlusconi and the centre-right over reforms.

D'Alema and Berlusconi agreed at a meeting on Tuesday that talks over the planned commission should be put off until parliament finished examining the 1997 budget. The financial bill has to be passed into law by the end of the year.
The right wants to introduce a presidential-style government and hardright leader Gianfranco Fini has demanded a guarantee that the proposed commission will move in this direction.
Refoundation and other government supporters, including the centrist Popular Party, are opposed to such an electoral system.
Politicians have talked for 15 years about the need to modernise Italy's 1948 constitution and end the history of revolving-door governments.
